newsitem.title: USA: CIA chief plays down Saddam's retaliatory options.
newsitem.headline: CIA chief plays down Saddam's retaliatory options.

text.p: Iraq, one of seven states accused by the United States of sponsoring terrorism, has no easy way to retaliate for U.S. cruise missile strikes against southern Iraqi military targets, CIA Director John Deutch said on Thursday.
Deutch said he did not believe Iraqi President Saddam Hussein had "an easy and immediate way to respond" to the firing of 44 missiles this week.

"But as we have seen in the past, he is going to continue to find a way of causing trouble in this region," Deutch said in reply to a question after a speech on U.S. efforts to penetrate foreign terrorist groups.
Earlier on Thursday, Deutch said Iraqi troops appeared to be withdrawing from a Western-protected Kurdish safehaven in the north of the country after the U.S. missile strikes.

But he said later that Iraq, with or without Saddam Hussein, would continue to be a problem and could pose future threats not only to the Kurds but to oil-rich neighbours like Saudi Arabia and Kuwait.
"It's not only Saddam Hussein, it's the regime that he's part of, the immediate group that he's part of," he said.

In his speech at Georgetown University, Deutch said the Central Intelligence Agency had "substantially increased" use of secret agents to pierce foreign terrorist groups and their alleged state sponsors, such as Iraq.
"The gain in the past 18 months far exceeds previous achievements," he said.
Thanks to these agents, the CIA has "an outstanding and growing" capability to uncover the secrets of targeted groups and "the countries that offer them sanctuary or support," Deutch said.
Beside Iraq, the United States lists Cuba, Iran, Libya, North Korea, Sudan and Syria as sponsors of terrorism.

Secrets gleaned by the CIA and the Federal Bureau of Investigation "conclusively" showed that Saddam was behind an alleged Iraqi plot to kill former U.S. President George Bush during a 1993 visit to Kuwait, the CIA chief said.

Deutch said radical Islamic fundamentalist groups were the chief threats. He named Hizbollah, the Iranian-inspired "Party of God;" the Egyptian opposition Islamic Group; and Hamas, a Palestinian fundamentalist group with ties to Syria and Iran.

Despite the stepped-up intelligence focus on thwarting foreign guerrillas, "we must anticipate new attempts against American citizens, against our troops and facilities, both here and abroad," he said.
Deutch announced a four-point programme to strengthen U.S. spy agencies' counter-terrorism capabilities at President Bill Clinton's request.

A new "foreign terrorism warning group" at the intelligence community's Counterterrorist Centre, which pools CIA information with that of sister spy outfits such as the National Security Agency, will review intelligence from all sources to warn of possible foreign terrorist attacks.
The CIA is also sending "a significant number" of additional case officers overseas and boosting the number of officers assigned to the Counterterrorist Centre, he said.

In addition, he said U.S. spy agencies were expanding intelligence support for protecting military facilities. A total of 24 Americans have been killed in two bombings in Saudi Arabia since last November. Terrorism fears have also been heightened by the suspicious explosion of TWA Flight 800 on July 17.

Finally, U.S. spy agencies were increasing their ability to "act forcefully against terrorists worldwide," Deutch said. Without disclosing details, he said the idea was to give the president "more options for action" to "preempt, disrupt and defeat" international terrorism.
